hook: Forty, and earning $8K a month? Fidelity says you should have $288,000 saved. (beat, presenter E, Eric voice)
caption:
40 and earning $8,000 a month? Fidelity's guideline says you should have $288,000 saved. Find your age:
30: $96,000 · 40: $288,000 · 50: $576,000 · 60: $768,000 · 67: $960,000
(1x salary by 30, 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, 10x by 67.)

The guideline assumes you save 15% of your pay every year from age 25, with your 401(k) and any employer match counting. Starting at 40? 15% of $8,000 is $1,200 a month: $388,800 by 67 before any investment growth.

It only happens if it leaves on payday. Then the rest gets one daily number that adjusts when you overspend.

Save first. Then spend what's safe.

Source: Fidelity Viewpoints, "How much should I have saved?" A guideline, not a rule; not financial advice.

hook: Keep telling yourself "I should really save more," but your savings haven't moved in months? (Study Reel S1, faceless diagram format, belief-first hook bet #7, Jessica voice, no music)
caption:
Keep telling yourself "I should really save more" while your savings don't move? A reminder to save did nothing in this study. Naming the goal did.

Economists tested monthly savings reminders with new savers at banks in Bolivia, Peru and the Philippines. In Peru, reminders that named the specific thing people were saving for raised savings by an estimated 16% compared with no reminder. Reminders that didn't name it had no effect. (Field experiments with new savers.)

Try it: set a monthly reminder on your phone that names the goal. Not "Remember to save." "Save for Paris in July." Saving for a few things? One reminder for each.

Study: Karlan, McConnell, Mullainathan & Zinman, Management Science, 2016. Link in the comments.

hook: Paying seventy dollars or more a month for a gym you barely go to? (Study Reel S7 v2: research-backed money tip #4)
caption:
Divide your gym bill by how many times you actually went.

Economists followed 7,752 members of three US gyms over three years. People on monthly plans over $70 paid, on average, 70% more than paying per visit would have cost for the visits they actually made. People overestimated how often they'd go. (Three gyms, one study.)

Your savings account probably pays you $1 a year on $10,000. Here's where to park savings you can't afford to lose, ranked.

S: Series I bonds, 5.51% (bought Nov 2026–Apr 2027). Rises with inflation. Catch: locked 12 months, you lose 3 months' interest if you cash out before 5 years, and it's $10K per person per year (so $20K for a couple).

If you're a parent, your emergency fund at a big bank probably earns $1 a year on $10,000. Where to park it instead, ranked:

S: Series I bonds, 5.51% (bought Nov 2026–Apr 2027). Rises with inflation. Catch: locked 12 months, 3 months' interest lost if cashed before 5 years, $10K per person per year.
A: High-yield savings (Vio Bank, Pibank), 4.40% APY. FDIC insured, out any day.
B: Robinhood cash sweep, 3.6% APY, only with Robinhood Gold ($5 a month): about $300 a year on $10K after the fee.
F: Standard savings at Chase or Wells Fargo, 0.01% (Wells Fargo's Platinum Savings pays more, but only on $25K+).

Rates as of Nov 27, 2026; they change often. Not financial advice; we're not paid by anyone on this list. Sources in the comments.

Send this to whoever still keeps their savings at Chase or Wells Fargo 🏦

hook: I built a budgeting app. Still blew my budget, 3 months in a row. (Real Numbers ep 01, founder's own screenshots)
caption:
I built a budgeting app. And I still went over budget three months in a row.

My monthly flexible spending budget: $2,000.

September: $2,993
October: $2,859
November: $3,032 (month to date)

That's $2,884 over budget. In the same three months I saved $1,000 first, every month: $3,000. The overspending almost cancelled it out.

So I'm running an experiment in December. Groceries stay the same. Dining out, shopping and entertainment get $400, combined.

No perfect budgets. No made-up numbers. Real screenshots from my own DivvyUpp account.

I'll share the real results in January. Anyone else doing a December spending challenge?

hook: Couples given a joint bank account stayed just as happy. (S10 V2: result first, lines split by 4.6 s, 20 s)
caption:
Couples given a joint bank account stayed just as happy. Separate accounts? Less happy, two years later.

In a two-year experiment, 230 engaged or newly married couples were randomly given a joint account, separate accounts, or their own choice. The joint-account couples kept their relationship quality and fought less about money; the others showed the usual decline. (About 1 in 5 couples dropped out, and the researchers don't say merge everything.)

Try it: open one shared account for shared costs, and keep your own too.

Study: Olson, Rick, Small & Finkel, Journal of Consumer Research, 2023. Link in the comments.

Send this to your partner, and set it up together 🤝
